name: Angkor Wat
why: Published research used decorrelation stretch to clarify faint paintings of boats, animals, deities and buildings on the temple walls.
photo: Close, evenly lit color photographs of faded painted wall sections, including adjacent unpainted stone.
caveat: A carved relief and a surviving paint trace are different kinds of evidence. Match any interpretation to the original photograph.
sourceLabel: Tan et al., The hidden paintings of Angkor Wat, Antiquity (2014)

name: Göreme / Cappadocia
why: Surviving red motifs and figurative frescoes in rock-hewn churches offer color information on a painted surface. The included photograph focuses on worn red decoration.
photo: Close, evenly lit original photographs of worn painted sections, with some adjacent surface.
caveat: Surface damage alone does not identify who caused it or why. The photograph may include conservation work.
sourceLabel: UNESCO, Göreme National Park and the Rock Sites of Cappadocia

name: Chehel Sotoun
why: The featured high-resolution photograph includes a painted narrative scene and worn ornamental borders. Try a border fit where pigment is patchy.
photo: Worn border details and original color documentation from before and after conservation.
caveat: The painting is historic, not prehistoric. Brilliant areas may offer little hidden detail. Do not infer intentional erasure or original hues from false colors.
sourceLabel: Amir Pashaei, original photograph and metadata

name: Bhimbetka
why: Surviving painted figures and faint neighboring traces make this a strong material match. A 17.9-megapixel photograph of Rock Shelter 8 is included.
photo: Close color views of the painted panel, preserving faint edges and some surrounding substrate.
caveat: Different paint layers, weathering and mineral staining can separate in similar ways. The app cannot date overlapping figures.
sourceLabel: UNESCO, Rock Shelters of Bhimbetka

name: Greek marble sphinx
why: The museum records surviving red, black and blue pigment on this original sphinx. The included open-access image supports an experiment on actual pigment traces.
photo: Close photographs of the wing, face and hair; fit to the sculpture rather than its studio backdrop.
caveat: Documented pigment is not a published test of this app. False colors do not reproduce the ancient palette. Avoid painted modern reconstructions as input.
sourceLabel: The Met, marble capital and finial in the form of a sphinx

name: Pompeii / House of the Vettii
why: The included Cyparissus image shows worn pigment and pale contours, providing a closer painted-surface example than a room overview.
photo: Straight-on high-resolution color photographs with the painting filling the frame.
caveat: Missing plaster cannot be recovered by color enhancement. Check conservation records before interpreting unusual boundaries.
sourceLabel: Original Cyparissus fresco photograph and metadata

name: Beni Hasan
why: A published DStretch study clarified obscure animal details in Egyptian tomb paintings, making this a direct precedent for photographic pigment enhancement.
photo: Tightly framed painted animals, outlines and faded details, with the wall evenly illuminated.
caveat: Compare with epigraphic records and conservation history before interpreting an unusual shape.
sourceLabel: Evans and Mourad, DStretch and Egyptian tomb paintings (2018)

name: Cueva San Borjitas
why: Jon Harman's algorithm description demonstrates enhanced pictographs here, including faint color differences in overlapping figures.
photo: Original color images of painted panels, with enough surrounding rock to compare pigment and substrate.
caveat: This app uses regularized RGB stretching; it does not reproduce DStretch's custom YDS or YBK presets.
sourceLabel: Jon Harman, DStretch algorithm description and examples

name: Tule River Painted Rock
why: The technique's author includes Tule River Painted Rock among his before-and-after rock-art demonstrations.
photo: Existing, permission-cleared close photographs of painted elements and their surrounding stone.
caveat: Use community-approved imagery and interpretation. Custom DStretch color-space examples may differ from this RGB implementation.
sourceLabel: Jon Harman, Tule River Painted Rock examples

name: Pyramid of Unas
why: The included image contains visibly colored inscriptions against stone. Their photographic color separation makes it a useful candidate for testing settings.
photo: Straight-on images of inscribed wall sections; include both colored and faint neighboring signs.
caveat: This study has not established new text or identified pigments. Shading in carved signs also changes color values.
sourceLabel: Aidan McRae Thomson, source photograph and metadata

name: Pompeii
why: The House of Menander example has faded wall decoration and surrounding plaster, a useful pairing for testing color differences on a selected surface.
photo: Close color photographs of faded painted walls, ideally with uniform light and minimal glare.
caveat: Weathering, plaster patches and conservation work can all produce distinct false colors.
sourceLabel: Marco Ober, House of Menander source photograph

name: Mogao Caves
why: UNESCO documents an extensive collection of cave murals. Faded painted details are a plausible target for color enhancement; this listing does not claim documented DStretch use here.
photo: Licensed archival color photographs of mural details, with capture and conservation information when available.
caveat: Check whether an image depicts an original surface, restoration, reconstruction or replica.
sourceLabel: UNESCO, Mogao Caves

name: Ajanta Caves
why: The caves' surviving wall paintings make close photographs of faded pigment a plausible application, based on the material rather than a verified DStretch case study.
photo: Original color close-ups of painted wall details with consistent illumination.
caveat: Strong exposure differences and surface deterioration can overwhelm small pigment differences.
sourceLabel: UNESCO, Ajanta Caves

name: Bonampak
why: INAH documents richly painted interior rooms and a history of conservation. Photographs of faint mural passages may be useful candidates for pigment separation.
photo: Permission-cleared color documentation of original mural surfaces, with dates and conservation context.
caveat: Prefer authorized archival images with conservation records and permission to make and share derivatives.
sourceLabel: INAH, Bonampak archaeological site

name: Tassili n'Ajjer
why: UNESCO documents a major collection of rock paintings and engravings. Painted panels with faint surviving pigment are a plausible fit for this color-based technique.
photo: Licensed, unedited color photographs of painted panels rather than distant landscape views.
caveat: The recommendation concerns painted surfaces. Unpainted engraving geometry usually calls for lighting-based or 3D documentation instead.
sourceLabel: UNESCO, Tassili n'Ajjer

name: Cueva de las Manos
why: Multiple surviving pigment colors and overlapping hand stencils make a useful comparison across painted areas.
photo: Original color views of faint stencils and adjacent unpainted surface, with even exposure.
caveat: Color differences alone do not establish the sequence or dates of overlapping paintings.
sourceLabel: UNESCO, Cueva de las Manos

name: Cliff Palace / Mesa Verde
why: NPS documents colored plaster, red triangles and geometric motifs in a Cliff Palace room. Painted interior walls are the target, rather than distant views of masonry.
photo: Permission-cleared, high-resolution color documentation of the mural. The NPS reference includes a historic monochrome image and a color comparison.
caveat: No suitable high-resolution original was cleared in this pass. The small reference is not presented as a high-resolution study image.
sourceLabel: National Park Service, wall-painting artifact record

name: Pompeii / Villa of the Mysteries
why: A 24-megapixel example allows selected-area fitting on a richly painted wall and its worn passages.
photo: Close color originals of faint passages, and dated photographs documenting conservation.
caveat: The scene is already visible. Enhancement explores surviving differences, not newly discovered figures or the original palette.
sourceLabel: Original Villa of the Mysteries photograph and metadata

name: Great Pyramid interior
why: The included image demonstrates strong color differences under mixed artificial lighting. It is useful for learning the app's limits, with no new marking established.
photo: Well-exposed stone details under consistent lighting, ideally repeated with a color reference.
caveat: Lighting and mineral variation dominate many views. Enhanced patches do not establish paint, writing, age or human intent.
sourceLabel: Ovedc, Great Pyramid interior source photograph

name: Titanic wreck interior
why: NOAA's bathroom photograph is useful for exploring how corrosion and surviving surfaces separate into false colors, with much lower confidence in historical interpretation.
photo: Well-lit original color frames from documented expeditions; preserve the source's native resolution.
caveat: Water absorption, illumination, compression and dark-region noise dominate. This is not underwater color recovery or a way to reveal covered rooms.
sourceLabel: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Titanic bathtub photograph
